title: Identity & Access Management
description: SSO/LDAP integration, RBAC for AI systems, service accounts, and enterprise-grade audit logging.

lessons.title: SSO and LDAP Integration
lessons.description: An enterprise AI system doesn't get its own separate login — it plugs into identity infrastructure that already exists.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why enterprise AI systems integrate with existing identity infrastructure rather than managing their own user accounts.

sections.title: 🔑 Single Sign-On (SSO): one identity, many systems
sections.content: **SSO** lets a user authenticate once with a central identity provider and gain access to multiple connected systems without logging in separately to each — directly extending the OAuth concepts from the App Dev course's authentication lesson to an organization-wide scale, where dozens or hundreds of internal systems all trust the same central identity provider rather than each managing its own user database.

sections.title: 📇 LDAP and directory services
sections.content: Many enterprises maintain a central directory (via **LDAP** or a similar protocol) listing every employee, their group memberships, and their organizational role — a new AI system integrating with this directory, rather than maintaining its own separate user list, means access changes (a new hire, a departure, a role change) propagate automatically instead of needing manual updates in yet another disconnected system.

sections.title: 🚫 Why maintaining a separate user database is a real liability
sections.content: An AI system with its own separate login system means someone has to remember to deprovision that specific system when an employee leaves — a step that's easy to forget precisely because it's one extra manual task among many, and a forgotten deprovisioning step is exactly the kind of access-control gap the next lesson's RBAC material is meant to prevent from having consequences.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Building a new AI system's authentication as a standalone user database instead of integrating with existing identity infrastructure.** As the code example shows, this creates a silent liability — access doesn't automatically follow an employee's actual status, and deprovisioning becomes an easily forgotten manual step.

**Assuming SSO integration is a one-time setup with no ongoing responsibility.** Directory schemas, group structures, and identity provider configurations can change over time — an integration that isn't periodically re-verified can quietly drift out of sync with how the organization's identity system actually works.

**Treating LDAP/SSO integration as purely a security nicety rather than an operational necessity at scale.** Manually managing user access for an AI system used by hundreds or thousands of employees doesn't scale — the automatic propagation SSO/LDAP integration provides is what makes access management tractable at that size.

questions.question: What does Single Sign-On (SSO) let a user do?
options: Authenticate once with a central identity provider and gain access to multiple connected systems without separate logins
Log in separately to every single system with a unique password for each
Bypass authentication entirely for any system
Only access one system per day regardless of how many they're authorized for
questions.explanation: SSO's core value is centralizing authentication so a single login grants access across many trusted, connected systems.

questions.question: Why is integrating a new AI system with an existing LDAP directory preferable to maintaining a separate user list?
options: Access changes like new hires, departures, or role changes propagate automatically instead of requiring manual updates in a disconnected system
LDAP integration is always technically simpler than building any login system from scratch
Separate user databases are required by most compliance frameworks
LDAP integration eliminates the need for any authentication whatsoever
questions.explanation: Centralizing identity means the AI system inherits the organization's existing, actively-maintained access records rather than needing its own parallel, easily-forgotten system.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `directory_system.can_login("bob")` return `False` after Bob's departure, while `separate_system.can_login("bob")` still returns `True`?
options: Because `directory_system` reads from the shared `central_directory` dict, which was updated immediately, while `separate_system` reads from its own `self.local_users` dict, which nobody updated
Because `separate_system` was deleted along with Bob's account
Because `directory_system` has a bug that always returns `False`
Because Bob's account still exists in the `central_directory`
questions.explanation: `DirectoryIntegratedSystem.can_login` checks `central_directory` directly, so the update to it is immediately visible; `SeparateUserDatabase.can_login` checks its own independent `local_users` dict, which nobody updated when Bob left.

questions.question: In the code example, what does updating `central_directory["bob"] = "deprovisioned"` demonstrate?
options: That a single update to the shared, central source of truth is enough to revoke access for any system checking that same source directly — no per-system manual step required
That deprovisioning Bob requires updating every system individually regardless of integration
That `central_directory` has no effect on either system's login behavior
That `separate_system`'s access is also revoked automatically by this update
questions.explanation: The one-line update to `central_directory` alone is sufficient to revoke `directory_system`'s access for Bob, illustrating the automatic-propagation benefit of directory integration — no such automatic propagation exists for `separate_system`.

questions.question: What does the contrast between `DirectoryIntegratedSystem` and `SeparateUserDatabase` in the code example illustrate about access-control risk?
options: That both systems handle deprovisioning identically

That a system relying on its own separate user list can silently retain a departed employee's access, purely because nobody remembered to update it, while directory integration avoids that risk by construction
That directory integration is always slower than a separate user database
That separate user databases are always more secure
questions.explanation: The code example makes concrete exactly the liability the lesson describes in prose: manual deprovisioning is an easily-missed step, and directory integration removes the need for it entirely.

questions.question: What real risk does a separate, disconnected login system for an AI application create?
options: Someone has to remember to deprovision that specific system when an employee leaves, which is an easily forgotten manual step
Separate login systems are always more secure than centralized identity
Disconnected systems automatically sync with the central directory with no extra effort
Disconnected login systems eliminate all access-control risk
questions.explanation: A parallel, disconnected user system depends on someone remembering an extra manual deprovisioning step — exactly the kind of gap that centralized identity integration avoids.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against building a new AI system's authentication as a standalone user database instead of integrating with existing identity infrastructure?
options: Because, as the code example shows, this creates a silent liability where access doesn't automatically follow an employee's actual status
Because standalone user databases are technically impossible to build
Because standalone databases are always slower to query than a central directory
Because integration with existing identity infrastructure is required by every programming language
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section states this directly, and the code example demonstrates concretely how the liability manifests — a departed employee retaining access purely due to a missed manual step.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating LDAP/SSO integration as purely a security nicety rather than an operational necessity at scale?
options: Because manually managing user access for an AI system used by hundreds or thousands of employees doesn't scale — automatic propagation is what makes access management tractable at that size
Because LDAP/SSO integration has no relationship to operational scale at all
Because manual access management scales better than automated propagation
Because security niceties are never worth implementing in an enterprise system
questions.explanation: The lesson frames this integration as a practical scaling necessity, not just a security best practice — manual management becomes untenable well before an organization reaches enterprise scale.

lessons.title: RBAC for AI Systems
lessons.description: Not every employee who can log in should be able to do everything the system can do.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain how role-based access control applies specifically to an enterprise AI system's distinct capabilities.

sections.title: 🎭 RBAC: permissions tied to roles, not individuals
sections.content: **Role-based access control (RBAC)** assigns permissions to roles (like "data scientist," "compliance reviewer," "end user") rather than to individual people directly, and users are assigned to one or more roles — changing what a person can do means changing their role assignment, not editing permissions for that person one by one.

sections.title: 🤖 What roles look like for an AI system specifically
sections.content:
- An **end user** might only be able to query a deployed model.
- A **data scientist** might additionally be able to view training data and trigger a fine-tuning job (Fine-Tuning course).
- An **administrator** might be able to change which model version is deployed to production.
- A **compliance reviewer** might have read-only access to audit logs and model cards (Eval & Security course) without any ability to change the system itself

Each role scoped to exactly what that function needs, echoing the least-privilege principle from the Cloud course's Linux permissions lesson.

sections.title: 🔀 RBAC intersects with the multi-tenancy from Module 2
sections.content: In a system serving multiple business units or external customers (the next module's subject), RBAC often needs a second dimension beyond just role — not just "what can this role do" but "what can this role do, within which tenant's data" — a data scientist role in one business unit shouldn't automatically see another business unit's training data just because the role name matches.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a simplified simulation of role-scoped permission checks, including the tenant dimension:

```python
ROLE_PERMISSIONS = {
    "end_user": {"query_model"},
    "data_scientist": {"query_model", "view_training_data", "trigger_finetune"},
    "administrator": {"query_model", "change_deployed_version"},
    "compliance_reviewer": {"view_audit_logs", "view_model_cards"},
}

def can_perform(role, action, requester_tenant, target_tenant):
    if requester_tenant != target_tenant:
        return False  # tenant boundary always wins, regardless of role
    return action in ROLE_PERMISSIONS.get(role, set())

print(can_perform("data_scientist", "trigger_finetune", "acme_corp", "acme_corp"))
print(can_perform("data_scientist", "trigger_finetune", "acme_corp", "other_corp"))
print(can_perform("compliance_reviewer", "change_deployed_version", "acme_corp", "acme_corp"))
```

The first call has matching tenants (`"acme_corp"` both times) and `"trigger_finetune"` is in `data_scientist`'s permission set, so it returns `True`. The second call has the same role and action but `requester_tenant="acme_corp"` while `target_tenant="other_corp"` — the tenant check fails immediately, returning `False` regardless of the role's permissions, exactly the tenant dimension described in the lesson. The third call has matching tenants, but `"change_deployed_version"` isn't in `compliance_reviewer`'s permission set (`{"view_audit_logs", "view_model_cards"}`), so it returns `False` — the role itself doesn't grant that action, independent of tenant.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Checking only role permissions without also checking the tenant boundary in a multi-tenant system.** As the code example shows, a role check alone can't prevent a legitimate data scientist role from being misused to access a different tenant's data — the tenant dimension has to be checked independently.

**Granting a role broader permissions than its actual function needs, for convenience.** Giving every role administrator-level access "just in case" defeats the purpose of RBAC's least-privilege design and turns a compromised low-privilege account into a much bigger risk.

**Editing permissions for individual users instead of updating role assignments.** One-off, per-person permission tweaks undermine RBAC's core value — a system with enough individual exceptions becomes just as hard to audit as if there were no roles at all.

questions.question: What does RBAC assign permissions to, rather than to individual people directly?
options: Roles, which users are then assigned to one or more of
Nothing; RBAC has no concept of permissions
Specific IP addresses only
Specific physical office locations only
questions.explanation: The core RBAC pattern is permissions attached to roles, with individuals gaining access by being assigned to a role, rather than having permissions configured person by person.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `can_perform("data_scientist", "trigger_finetune", "acme_corp", "other_corp")` return `False`?
options: Because `"trigger_finetune"` isn't in `data_scientist`'s permission set
Because `requester_tenant` ("acme_corp") doesn't match `target_tenant` ("other_corp"), so the function returns `False` immediately regardless of the role's permissions
Because `data_scientist` is not a valid role in `ROLE_PERMISSIONS`
Because the function always returns `False` on the second call
questions.explanation: `can_perform` checks `requester_tenant != target_tenant` first and returns `False` immediately if they differ — the role's permission set is never even consulted in that case.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `can_perform("compliance_reviewer", "change_deployed_version", "acme_corp", "acme_corp")` return `False`?
options: Because the tenants don't match
Because the tenants match, but `"change_deployed_version"` is not in `compliance_reviewer`'s permission set `{"view_audit_logs", "view_model_cards"}`
Because `compliance_reviewer` is not a defined role
Because `change_deployed_version` is not a valid action string
questions.explanation: With matching tenants, the function falls through to `action in ROLE_PERMISSIONS.get(role, set())`; `"change_deployed_version"` isn't in the compliance reviewer's permission set, so it returns `False`.

questions.question: What does the code example demonstrate about the relationship between role permissions and the tenant check?
options: That the tenant check is evaluated first and can override what a role's permissions would otherwise allow
That role permissions are checked before the tenant boundary in every case
That tenant and role checks are entirely independent and never interact
That the tenant check only applies to the `administrator` role
questions.explanation: `can_perform`'s tenant check runs first and short-circuits the function before the role's permission set is even examined — the tenant boundary takes precedence over what the role alone would permit.

questions.question: Why might a compliance reviewer role have read-only access to audit logs and model cards but no ability to change the system?
options: Because that role's function is oversight, not operation, so its permissions should be scoped to exactly what that function needs, following least-privilege
Because compliance reviewers should have unrestricted access to every part of the system
Because read-only access is technically impossible to implement in RBAC
Because compliance reviewers never need to see any system information at all
questions.explanation: Scoping each role's permissions to exactly its actual function is the least-privilege principle applied to role design, limiting risk without blocking legitimate work.

questions.question: Why does RBAC often need a tenant dimension in a multi-tenant enterprise AI system?
options: Because a role like 'data scientist' existing in one business unit shouldn't automatically grant visibility into another business unit's data just because the role name matches
Because multi-tenancy eliminates the need for any role-based permissions
Because tenants and roles are the exact same concept with no distinction
Because RBAC cannot function at all in a multi-tenant system
questions.explanation: Role alone isn't enough in a multi-tenant system — permissions need to be scoped both by what a role can do and which tenant's data that access applies to.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against checking only role permissions without also checking the tenant boundary?
options: Because, as the code example shows, a role check alone can't prevent a legitimate role from being misused to access a different tenant's data — the tenant dimension has to be checked independently
Because tenant checks are unnecessary once roles are properly defined
Because role permissions and tenant boundaries are the same check
Because tenant checks always make role checks redundant
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section reinforces exactly what the code example shows: role and tenant are separate dimensions, and skipping the tenant check leaves a real cross-tenant access gap.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against editing permissions for individual users instead of updating role assignments?
options: Because one-off, per-person permission tweaks undermine RBAC's core value, and a system with enough individual exceptions becomes just as hard to audit as having no roles at all
Because individual permission edits are technically impossible in any RBAC system
Because role assignments can never be changed once set
Because per-user exceptions always improve system security
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section is explicit that per-user exceptions erode the auditability RBAC is meant to provide, effectively recreating an unstructured permissions system role by role.

lessons.title: Service Accounts and API Access
lessons.description: Not every caller of an enterprise AI system is a human — machine-to-machine access needs its own identity model.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a service account is and why it needs different management practices than a human user account.

sections.title: 🤖 Service accounts: identity for non-human callers
sections.content: A **service account** represents a non-human caller — another internal system, an automated pipeline, a scheduled batch job — that needs to authenticate and access the AI system, using the API-key authentication model from the App Dev course's auth lesson, now specifically for internal service-to-service enterprise traffic rather than external API consumers.

sections.title: 🔄 Why service accounts need different lifecycle management
sections.content: A human employee's access naturally ties to their employment status through the SSO/LDAP integration from earlier in this module — when they leave, access disappears automatically. A service account has no such natural tie; it persists until someone explicitly decommissions it, which means unused or orphaned service accounts (belonging to a decommissioned pipeline nobody remembered to clean up) are a common, quiet source of unnecessary access risk in enterprise systems.

sections.title: 🔑 Scoping service account permissions tightly
sections.content: A service account should have exactly the permissions its specific automated task needs — a nightly batch job that only reads aggregated metrics shouldn't have write access to production model configuration, following the same least-privilege discipline this module has applied to both human roles and now machine identities.

sections.title: 📋 Inventory and periodic review
sections.content: Because service accounts don't naturally expire the way human access does, periodically auditing the full list of active service accounts — what they're for, whether they're still needed, whether their permissions are still appropriately scoped — is a necessary practice this module's audit-logging lesson will build on directly.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a simplified simulation of a service account inventory review, flagging accounts that are orphaned or over-scoped:

```python
service_accounts = [
    {"name": "nightly-metrics-job", "owning_pipeline_active": True, "permissions": {"read_metrics"}},
    {"name": "legacy-etl-pipeline", "owning_pipeline_active": False, "permissions": {"read_metrics", "write_config"}},
    {"name": "model-deploy-bot", "owning_pipeline_active": True, "permissions": {"read_metrics", "write_config", "deploy_model"}},
]

REQUIRED_PERMISSIONS = {
    "nightly-metrics-job": {"read_metrics"},
    "legacy-etl-pipeline": {"read_metrics", "write_config"},
    "model-deploy-bot": {"deploy_model"},
}

def audit_service_accounts(accounts):
    findings = []
    for acct in accounts:
        if not acct["owning_pipeline_active"]:
            findings.append(f"{acct['name']}: ORPHANED -- owning pipeline no longer active")
            continue
        required = REQUIRED_PERMISSIONS[acct["name"]]
        extra = acct["permissions"] - required
        if extra:
            findings.append(f"{acct['name']}: OVER-SCOPED -- has unnecessary permissions {extra}")
    return findings

for finding in audit_service_accounts(service_accounts):
    print(finding)
```

`nightly-metrics-job` has an active owning pipeline and `permissions == REQUIRED_PERMISSIONS[...]` exactly, so `extra` is an empty set and it produces no finding. `legacy-etl-pipeline` has `owning_pipeline_active=False`, so the loop flags it as `"ORPHANED"` immediately via `continue`, without even checking its permissions. `model-deploy-bot` has an active pipeline, but its actual `permissions` set (`{"read_metrics", "write_config", "deploy_model"}`) minus its `REQUIRED_PERMISSIONS` (`{"deploy_model"}`) leaves `extra = {"read_metrics", "write_config"}` — flagged as `"OVER-SCOPED"`, holding two permissions it doesn't actually need for its stated task.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Never revisiting service account permissions after initial setup.** As the code example's `model-deploy-bot` shows, a service account can accumulate more permissions than it needs over time (often from copy-pasting a broader existing account's config) without anyone noticing, since there's no natural review trigger the way employment status provides for human accounts.

**Not tracking which pipeline or system owns each service account.** Without that ownership record, an orphaned account — like `legacy-etl-pipeline` in the example — can go unnoticed indefinitely, since there's no employee departure event to prompt someone to check it.

**Sharing one service account's credentials across multiple unrelated automated tasks for convenience.** This defeats tight scoping entirely — the shared account ends up needing the union of every task's permissions, and a compromise or bug in any one task has blast radius across all of them.

questions.question: What is a service account, in the context of enterprise access management?
options: An identity representing a non-human caller, like an internal system, automated pipeline, or scheduled batch job
A special type of human employee account with extra privileges
A temporary guest account for external visitors
A backup copy of a human user's account
questions.explanation: Service accounts exist specifically to give non-human, automated callers their own identity and access, distinct from human user accounts.

questions.question: In the code example, why is `legacy-etl-pipeline` flagged as "ORPHANED" without its permissions even being checked?
options: Because `owning_pipeline_active` is `False` for it, so `audit_service_accounts` appends the orphaned finding and hits `continue`, skipping the permission-scoping check entirely for that account
Because `legacy-etl-pipeline` has no entry in `REQUIRED_PERMISSIONS`
Because its permissions set is empty
Because `nightly-metrics-job` is checked first and consumes the loop
questions.explanation: The function checks `owning_pipeline_active` first; when it's `False`, it appends the orphaned finding and immediately `continue`s to the next account, never reaching the `extra = acct["permissions"] - required` scoping check for that account.

questions.question: In the code example, what is `extra` for `model-deploy-bot`, and what does it represent?
options: An empty set, since `model-deploy-bot` needs no permissions
`{"read_metrics", "write_config"}`, computed as `acct["permissions"] - required` — permissions the account holds beyond what `REQUIRED_PERMISSIONS` says it actually needs
`{"deploy_model"}`, the permission it's missing
The full set of all three permissions
questions.explanation: `extra = acct["permissions"] - required` subtracts the required set `{"deploy_model"}` from the actual permissions `{"read_metrics", "write_config", "deploy_model"}`, leaving `{"read_metrics", "write_config"}` as unnecessary extras.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `nightly-metrics-job` produce no finding?
options: Because its `owning_pipeline_active` is `False`
Because its owning pipeline is active and its `permissions` set exactly matches `REQUIRED_PERMISSIONS["nightly-metrics-job"]`, leaving `extra` as an empty set, which is falsy in the `if extra:` check
Because it isn't included in the `service_accounts` list
Because `audit_service_accounts` only checks the first two accounts
questions.explanation: With an active pipeline and `permissions == required` exactly, `extra` computes to an empty set, and `if extra:` is `False` for an empty set, so no finding is appended for this account.

questions.question: What does the `audit_service_accounts` function's two-part check (ownership status, then permission scope) illustrate about the lesson's inventory review practice?
options: That a periodic review needs to catch both accounts that should no longer exist at all (orphaned) and accounts that exist appropriately but hold more access than their task requires (over-scoped) — two distinct kinds of risk
That only orphaned accounts are ever a security concern
That over-scoped accounts are always also orphaned
That the two checks are redundant with each other
questions.explanation: The function's structure mirrors the lesson's point that service account risk comes in (at least) two distinct forms — accounts that should be decommissioned, and accounts that are legitimate but too broadly scoped.

questions.question: Why do service accounts pose a distinct access-management risk compared to human user accounts?
options: They have no natural tie to an employment status, so they persist until someone explicitly decommissions them, making orphaned accounts a common, quiet risk
Service accounts automatically expire after 24 hours with no further action needed
Service accounts cannot be granted any permissions at all
Human accounts never pose any access-management risk, unlike service accounts
questions.explanation: Unlike human accounts tied to employment status, service accounts lack a natural expiration trigger, so forgotten, orphaned accounts can quietly accumulate unnecessary access.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against never revisiting service account permissions after initial setup?
options: Because, as the `model-deploy-bot` example shows, a service account can accumulate more permissions than it needs over time without anyone noticing, since there's no natural review trigger like employment status provides
Because service account permissions are fixed at creation and cannot change
Because reviewing permissions always removes permissions the account actually needs
Because initial setup always grants the minimum necessary permissions with no risk of drift
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section connects directly to the code example's over-scoping finding — without periodic review, permission creep goes undetected indefinitely.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against sharing one service account's credentials across multiple unrelated automated tasks?
options: Because this defeats tight scoping — the shared account ends up needing the union of every task's permissions, and a compromise or bug in any one task has blast radius across all of them
Because shared credentials are technically impossible to configure
Because sharing credentials always improves system performance
Because each automated task requires its own separate physical server
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section explains that credential sharing forces over-broad permissions and expands the blast radius of any single task's compromise or bug to every other task sharing that account.

lessons.title: Audit Logging
lessons.description: When something goes wrong, 'who did what, when' needs to already be answerable — not reconstructed after the fact.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what an enterprise-grade audit log needs to capture and why it must be tamper-resistant.

sections.title: 📝 What belongs in an audit log
sections.content: **Who** (which user or service account) did **what** (queried the model, changed a configuration, accessed training data) **when** (a precise timestamp), and — for an AI system specifically — often **what the system's response or action was too**, not just that a request was made. This directly extends the accountability logging the Vector Databases course's closing security lesson and the App Dev course's securing-LLM-endpoints lesson both called for, now as a formal, comprehensive enterprise practice.

sections.title: 🔒 Tamper-resistance: the log has to be trustworthy
sections.content: An audit log that the same people it might implicate can freely edit or delete isn't a trustworthy record — enterprise audit logging typically writes to storage that's append-only or otherwise protected from modification by the very systems and accounts being logged, so the log remains a reliable record even in an investigation involving someone with broad system access.

sections.title: ⚖️ Audit logs serve both security and compliance
sections.content: Beyond helping diagnose a security incident (was this account compromised, what did the attacker actually do), audit logs are often a hard compliance requirement — many regulatory frameworks (covered more fully in the governance module) explicitly require the ability to answer "who accessed this specific sensitive data, when" for a defined retention period, not just as a nice-to-have practice.

sections.title: 🔗 Closing this module's arc
sections.content: This module moved from centralizing identity (SSO/LDAP), to scoping what each identity can do (RBAC), to accounting for non-human identities (service accounts), to finally recording what every identity actually did (audit logging) — a complete access-management lifecycle for an enterprise AI system.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Storing audit logs in the same mutable database the audited system itself can write to freely.** As the code example shows, if the system (or someone with its access) can delete or edit its own audit trail, the log's evidentiary value collapses exactly when it matters most — during an actual incident.

**Logging only that a request occurred, without the system's actual response or action.** For an AI system, knowing what the model returned or did is often essential to understanding the impact of an incident, not just that some interaction happened.

**Treating audit logging as purely a security feature with no compliance retention requirements considered.** Regulatory frameworks often mandate a specific minimum retention period for audit records — a log that's rotated out or deleted too early can fail a compliance requirement even if it was perfectly tamper-resistant while it existed.

questions.question: Beyond who did what and when, what does an audit log for an AI system often need to capture that a typical application's log might not?
options: The system's actual response or action, not just the fact that a request was made
The programming language the AI system was written in
The physical location of the data center
The user's personal email signature
questions.explanation: For an AI system, knowing what the model actually did or returned in response to a request is often as important as knowing that a request occurred at all, especially for accountability purposes.

questions.question: In the code example, what happens when `audit_log.delete_entry(0)` is called?
options: The entry is silently removed with no error
It raises `PermissionError("audit log storage does not support deletion")`, and the entry remains in the log afterward
It returns `False` without modifying the log
It deletes the entire log, not just the one entry
questions.explanation: `AppendOnlyLog.delete_entry` is implemented to unconditionally `raise PermissionError`, so calling it always fails and the underlying `_entries` list is never modified.

questions.question: In the code example, what is `mutable_log.entries` after `del mutable_log.entries[0]` runs?
options: Still contains the original entry, unchanged
An empty list — the deletion succeeds because nothing in `MutableLog` protects `entries` from direct external mutation
Raises a `PermissionError`, identical to the append-only log's behavior
Contains two entries instead of one
questions.explanation: `MutableLog` exposes `self.entries` as a plain, unprotected list; `del mutable_log.entries[0]` directly removes the only entry with no error, leaving an empty list.

questions.question: What does the contrast between `AppendOnlyLog` and `MutableLog` in the code example demonstrate about tamper-resistance?
options: That both classes behave identically under a deletion attempt
That tamper-resistance is a structural property of how the log is implemented — one class refuses deletion outright by design, while the other allows silent, untracked mutation
That mutable logs are always faster to query than append-only logs
That append-only logs cannot record any data at all
questions.explanation: The two classes differ only in whether deletion is structurally blocked; that difference alone is what separates a trustworthy audit record from one an attacker with access could quietly erase.

questions.question: Why does an audit log need to be tamper-resistant, ideally append-only?
options: Because a log the implicated parties could freely edit or delete wouldn't be a trustworthy record, especially in an investigation involving someone with broad access
Because tamper-resistant logs are technically easier to build than mutable ones
Because append-only storage is always cheaper than any alternative
Because tamper-resistance has no relationship to the log's trustworthiness
questions.explanation: The whole value of an audit log as evidence depends on it being resistant to modification by the very accounts or systems it might need to implicate.

questions.question: Beyond security incident diagnosis, what other purpose do audit logs commonly serve in an enterprise?
options: Satisfying regulatory compliance requirements that explicitly mandate the ability to answer who accessed specific sensitive data and when
Replacing the need for any RBAC or service account management
Automatically fixing any security vulnerabilities they detect
Eliminating the need for any SSO or LDAP integration
questions.explanation: Audit logging often exists not just as good security practice but as a formal, explicit requirement under various regulatory compliance frameworks.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against storing audit logs in the same mutable database the audited system can write to freely?
options: Because, as the code example shows, if the system or someone with its access can delete or edit the audit trail, the log's evidentiary value collapses exactly when it matters most — during an actual incident
Because mutable databases are always slower than append-only storage
Because audit logs are never actually needed during a security incident
Because mutable databases cannot store timestamps
questions.explanation: The common mistakes section directly echoes the code example's point: shared mutability between the audited system and its own audit trail defeats the log's purpose right when it's needed most.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating audit logging as purely a security feature with no compliance retention requirements considered?
options: Because regulatory frameworks often mandate a specific minimum retention period, and a log rotated out or deleted too early can fail a compliance requirement even if it was tamper-resistant while it existed
Because compliance frameworks never actually require audit log retention
Because retention requirements only apply to non-AI systems
Because tamper-resistance alone always satisfies every compliance requirement automatically
questions.explanation: The lesson notes audit logs serve compliance as well as security — retention duration is a distinct requirement from tamper-resistance, and missing it can create a compliance gap independent of the log's integrity.
